item.title: LLM-assisted review: preparing PRs and managing findings
item.description: Sharing practices without losing diversity The session considered whether tighter integration of large language models (LLMs) into development and review could help the project ship faster. One question was whether contributors should distill and share best practices to avoid duplicating effort. Participants also recognized a tension: standardizing approaches could reduce wasted work, but a diversity of strategies may uncover problems that a single shared approach misses. A “spell checker” analogy was raised as a way to frame LLM assistance.

item.title: Quantum Priorities
item.description: Proactive versus reactive approaches The discussion distinguished two broad categories of quantum-resistance work: Proactive measures: introducing output types and cryptography that allow users to migrate before a quantum threat materializes. Reactive measures: recovery or migration mechanisms used after “Q-day,” including scenarios where vulnerable funds have already been frozen. Many participants expressed little interest in the reactive category, preferring to focus on migration before an emergency. This was a preference expressed during the session, not a recorded decision to exclude recovery research.

item.title: How To Fix addr Relay and addrman
item.description: Scope and observed behavior The session examined address relay and its interaction with the address manager, addrman. The primary question was not how nodes select peers, but how easily a newly reachable node can obtain inbound connections. A new node advertises its address, but that address must enter other nodes’ address managers before they can select it for an outbound connection. DNS seeds help new nodes find outbound peers; they do not directly solve the problem of attracting inbound connections.

item.title: Erlay
item.description: Scope of the discussion I want to recap what we discussed in Barcelona, cover the state of the pull request, and raise some questions that came up during the reimplementation. In Barcelona, we discussed changing the approach. Rather than using Erlay primarily to minimize bandwidth, the idea is to use it more as a fallback for eclipse protection. We have focused on hybrid connections for a few years, trying to make the trade-offs worth the complexity.

item.title: Mutation Testing
item.description: Surviving mutants and test coverage The session focused on the challenge of investigating surviving—or “live”—mutants: generated code changes that the test suite does not detect. Participants reported that bitcoincore.space listed 431 surviving mutants, including many in consensus code. Two had been verified as meaningful gaps, and pull requests had been opened to add tests that detected them. Many other candidates remained to be investigated. The raw count does not directly measure the number of testing gaps.

item.title: Private Broadcast

item.title: pruneassumevalid
item.description: Goal and proposed optimizations The proposal combines pruning with assumevalid to obtain the UTXO set as quickly as possible, reducing historical data downloads and unnecessary disk I/O. The starting argument was that, where assumevalid already skips script verification, a pruned node could avoid additional work: Downloading witness data. Building and saving undo data. Writing historical blocks to disk only to delete them shortly afterward. These were proposed optimizations, not a description of existing behavior.

item.title: QML GUI
item.description: Project status and the staging branch Let’s talk about the state of QML first. We have a preview app at bitcoincore.app. It builds from our latest development branch, and we have been getting great feedback. The main thing I want feedback on is the tracking issue, specifically the staging branch. We currently have two parallel tracks. In the gui-qml project, the qt6 branch has all the latest development, but it contains about 1,600 commits.

item.title: Silent Payment Sending
item.description: Scope and status The session covered ongoing work to merge silent payment sending support: constructing a transaction that pays a silent payment address. A list of related pull requests was referenced, but the notes do not include their identifiers. The discussion focused on the interactions with fee bumping, wallet persistence, coin selection, and compatibility when downgrading to an older version. RBF and the information the wallet must retain Supporting replace-by-fee (RBF) requires persisting additional information, including the recipient’s static payment code.

item.title: Bitcoin Core Developer Recruitment
item.description: What does Bitcoin Core need from new contributors? Motivation and independence The discussion emphasized several qualities that recruitment programs could look for: Intrinsic motivation: Why does someone want to contribute to Bitcoin Core? Self-direction and initiative: Bitcoin Core is not a conventional job with a manager assigning tasks. Practical experience: Contributors who actively use the software are more likely to identify meaningful problems. Communication skills: Contributors need to explain technical ideas and feedback effectively, particularly in pull request discussions.

item.title: Libmultiprocess: Windows support and client integration
item.description: Libmultiprocess: Windows support and client integration Scope The session covered Windows support for libmultiprocess and Bitcoin Core’s inter-process communication (IPC), together with the corresponding client-side work in sv2-tp. The notes identified three related pull requests and focused on compiler testing and a possible version 33 target. 1 Implementation work The work spans the underlying library, Bitcoin Core’s integration, and an application connecting to Core over IPC. Pull request Purpose libmultiprocess #231: Add Windows support Adds Windows support to the IPC library, including spawning child processes connected to their parent.

item.title: Wallet Rebroadcasting
item.description: Scope of the discussion There are two parts to this discussion. One is specifically about private broadcast and what I think is unexpected behavior. Interactions between wallet rebroadcasting and private broadcast raised the question of whether wallet rebroadcasting makes sense at all, particularly in the context of private broadcast. There are two questions: In the long term, what should we do about rebroadcasting? In the short term, should we mitigate this unexpected interaction with private broadcast?
